```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, knitr, kableExtra)

# Anchor all paths to the repository root, located by walking up from the
# working directory until references.bib is found. This is robust to how
# Quarto sets the execution directory under the manuscript/ project context.
find_root <- function(start = getwd()) {
  d <- normalizePath(start)
  while (!file.exists(file.path(d, "references.bib")) && dirname(d) != d) d <- dirname(d)
  d
}
ROOT <- find_root()
rp <- function(...) file.path(ROOT, ...)

# Corrected likelihood engine (dnorm-based get_ll and calc_bayes_factors) and
# the honest monitoring-index engine (slowdown_index: two-sample mean
# comparison + likelihood-ratio test). See R/bayes_factors.R,
# R/monitoring_index.R and the audit appendix audit/get_ll_fix_impact.qmd.
source(rp("R", "bayes_factors.R"))
source(rp("R", "monitoring_index.R"))

populations <- c("United Kingdom", "England", "Scotland", "Wales", "Northern Ireland")

# Actual e0 to 2024. Values to 2018 are the ONS single-year life tables (as
# used in the original paper); 2019-2024 are the historic estimates embedded in
# the 2024-based NPP expectation-of-life files, because ONS no longer publishes
# single-year life tables beyond 2020 (NOTES.md).
dta_e0 <- read_csv(rp("data", "e0_from_ons_allnations_extended.csv"),
                   show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(population %in% populations)

ch_e0_dta <- dta_e0 %>%
  group_by(population, sex) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(ch_e0 = e0 - lag(e0)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(ch_e0))

# --- Calibration window 1991-2010 (annual changes) --------------------------
calib <- ch_e0_dta %>%
  filter(between(year, 1991, 2010)) %>%
  group_by(population, sex) %>%
  summarise(mean_ch = mean(ch_e0), sd_ch = sd(ch_e0), .groups = "drop")

uk_calib_f <- calib %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom", sex == "female") %>% pull(mean_ch)
uk_calib_m <- calib %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom", sex == "male")   %>% pull(mean_ch)

# --- Decade means (UK) ------------------------------------------------------
uk_decades <- ch_e0_dta %>%
  filter(population == "United Kingdom") %>%
  mutate(dec = case_when(
    between(year, 1981, 1990) ~ "1980s",
    between(year, 1991, 2000) ~ "1990s",
    between(year, 2001, 2010) ~ "2000s",
    between(year, 2011, 2019) ~ "2011-19",
    between(year, 2020, 2024) ~ "2020-24"
  )) %>%
  filter(!is.na(dec)) %>%
  group_by(sex, dec) %>%
  summarise(m = mean(ch_e0), .groups = "drop")

uk_dec <- function(sx, d) uk_decades %>% filter(sex == sx, dec == d) %>% pull(m)

# --- Three observation-window variants (corrected engine) -------------------
variant_defs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~variant,          ~after_first, ~after_last, ~drop_years,
  "Pre-2020",        2011L,        2019L,       list(integer(0)),
  "Full series",     2011L,        2024L,       list(integer(0)),
  "COVID-excluded",  2011L,        2024L,       list(c(2020L, 2021L))
)

run_variant <- function(dta, after_first, after_last, drop_years) {
  d <- dta %>% filter(!year %in% drop_years[[1]])
  calc_bayes_factors(d, before_period = c(1991, 2010),
                     after_period = c(after_first, after_last), outcome_var = ch_e0)
}

bf_all <-
  ch_e0_dta %>%
  select(-e0, -source) %>%
  group_by(population, sex) %>%
  nest() %>%
  crossing(variant_defs) %>%
  mutate(bayes_df = pmap(list(data, after_first, after_last, drop_years), run_variant)) %>%
  select(population, sex, variant, bayes_df) %>%
  unnest(cols = c(bayes_df)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations),
         variant = factor(variant, levels = c("Pre-2020", "Full series", "COVID-excluded")))

bf_argmax <-
  bf_all %>%
  group_by(population, sex, variant) %>%
  slice_max(log_bf, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(population, sex, variant,
            slowdown_pct = 100 * (1 - perc),
            log10_bf = log_bf / log(10),
            bf = bayes_factor,
            mu_best = mu)

# Reproduction of the original paper's 2011-2018 window.
repro_1118 <-
  ch_e0_dta %>%
  filter(population == "United Kingdom") %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  nest() %>%
  mutate(bf = map(data, ~calc_bayes_factors(.x, c(1991, 2010), c(2011, 2018), ch_e0))) %>%
  select(sex, bf) %>% unnest(bf) %>%
  group_by(sex) %>% slice_max(log_bf, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>%
  transmute(sex, slowdown_pct = round(100 * (1 - perc)))
repro_f <- repro_1118 %>% filter(sex == "female") %>% pull(slowdown_pct)
repro_m <- repro_1118 %>% filter(sex == "male")   %>% pull(slowdown_pct)

# --- Monitoring-index likelihood-ratio test --------------------------------
# Primary inferential summary. slowdown_index() reports the two-sample mean
# comparison (rate_ratio, slowdown_pct), the LR test of "some slowdown" vs
# "no slowdown" (lr_stat, p_value), and the profile likelihood ratio (plr,
# the quantity earlier mislabelled a Bayes factor). The 2011-2018 window
# reproduces the original paper's headline exactly and is the primary
# inferential table; the pre-2020 (2011-2019) window is reported alongside to
# show the significance pattern is unchanged by adding 2019.
lr_index <- function(win) {
  ch_e0_dta %>%
    group_by(population, sex) %>% nest() %>%
    mutate(si = map(data, ~slowdown_index(.x, c(1991, 2010), win, ch_e0))) %>%
    select(population, sex, si) %>% unnest(si) %>% ungroup() %>%
    mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) %>%
    arrange(population, sex)
}
lr_1118 <- lr_index(c(2011, 2018))
lr_pre2020 <- lr_index(c(2011, 2019))

lr_get <- function(pop, sx, col, tbl = lr_1118)
  tbl %>% filter(population == pop, sex == sx) %>% pull({{ col }})
n_sig <- sum(lr_1118$p_value < 0.05)

# Non-independence of the two significant male cells: England is a large
# deterministic component of the UK aggregate, so the UK-male and England-male
# annual-change series are almost perfectly correlated.
uk_eng_m <- ch_e0_dta %>%
  filter(sex == "male", population %in% c("United Kingdom", "England")) %>%
  select(population, year, ch_e0) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = population, values_from = ch_e0)
cor_uk_eng_m <- cor(uk_eng_m$`United Kingdom`, uk_eng_m$England, use = "complete.obs")

# Headline (Pre-2020) and other UK variant values.
uk_arg <- bf_argmax %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom")
uk_val <- function(var, sx) round(uk_arg %>% filter(variant == var, sex == sx) %>% pull(slowdown_pct))
hl_f  <- uk_val("Pre-2020", "female"); hl_m  <- uk_val("Pre-2020", "male")
full_f <- uk_val("Full series", "female"); full_m <- uk_val("Full series", "male")
cov_f  <- uk_val("COVID-excluded", "female"); cov_m <- uk_val("COVID-excluded", "male")

# --- Persistence comparison against 2020-2024 (not a forecast validation) ---
pre2020_implied <- bf_argmax %>% filter(variant == "Pre-2020") %>%
  select(population, sex, implied_annual = mu_best)

observed_2024 <- ch_e0_dta %>%
  filter(between(year, 2020, 2024)) %>%
  group_by(population, sex) %>%
  summarise(obs_2020 = ch_e0[year == 2020],
            obs_mean_2022_24 = mean(ch_e0[between(year, 2022, 2024)]),
            obs_mean_2020_24 = mean(ch_e0), .groups = "drop")

validation_table <- pre2020_implied %>%
  left_join(observed_2024, by = c("population", "sex")) %>%
  mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) %>%
  arrange(population, sex)

uk_oos <- validation_table %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom")
oos_g <- function(sx, col) uk_oos %>% filter(sex == sx) %>% pull({{ col }})

# Overshoot of the recovered rate relative to the pre-2020 implied gain. By the
# monitoring-index identity the "pre-2020 implied gain" IS the 2011-2019 sample
# mean, so this compares a recovery-period mean against a calibration mean, not
# a genuine forecast against an outturn.
oos_overshoot <- function(sx)
  oos_g(sx, obs_mean_2022_24) / oos_g(sx, implied_annual)

# --- Monitoring-index benchmark vs ONS projection rounds --------------------
ons_projections_tidied <- read_rds(rp("data", "ons_projections", "all_tidied_2012_2024.rds"))

bf_benchmark <- pre2020_implied %>%
  transmute(population = as.character(population), sex, bf_mu = implied_annual)

ons_implied <-
  ons_projections_tidied %>%
  mutate(sex = case_when(sex == "f" ~ "female", sex == "m" ~ "male", TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>%
  filter(age == 0, year >= proj_year) %>%
  group_by(country, sex, proj_year) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(ch_e0 = ex - lag(ex)) %>%
  summarise(ons_mu = mean(ch_e0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(country = ifelse(country == "UK", "United Kingdom", country)) %>%
  rename(population = country, round = proj_year)

combined_long <-
  ons_implied %>%
  mutate(population = as.character(population)) %>%
  left_join(bf_benchmark, by = c("population", "sex")) %>%
  mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) %>%
  arrange(population, sex, round)

uk_cmp <- combined_long %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom")
uk_get <- function(sx, rd) uk_cmp %>% filter(sex == sx, round == rd) %>% pull(ons_mu)
bf_f <- bf_benchmark %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom", sex == "female") %>% pull(bf_mu)
bf_m <- bf_benchmark %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom", sex == "male")   %>% pull(bf_mu)

f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

**Background.** The UK Office for National Statistics (ONS) revises its national
life-expectancy projections every two years. Through the 2000s these
projections repeatedly *under*-estimated improvement and were successively
uprated; after period life expectancy at birth ($e_0$) stalled around 2010 they
began to *over*-estimate improvement and were successively downrated. This paper
sets out a transparent, rapidly-updatable monitoring index for the post-2010
slowdown, applies it to the extended $e_0$ series to 2024, and compares the
pre-pandemic estimate descriptively against the 2020–2024 outturn.

**Objective.** To quantify how far UK $e_0$ improvement has fallen below its
1991–2010 trend, to state what formal significance the data support, and to
reassess how optimistic successive ONS rounds have been.

**Methods.** Period $e_0$ was taken from the Human Mortality Database (HMD) for
international comparison and from the ONS for UK nations. The monitoring index is
a two-sample comparison of the mean annual $e_0$ change in a post-2010
observation window against the 1991–2010 calibration mean: the maximising
slowdown proportion equals the ratio of these two means. We report the point
slowdown, and a likelihood-ratio test of "some slowdown" against "no slowdown"
(Normal likelihood, calibration variance treated as known). An earlier version
framed the same quantity as a Bayes factor; it is more precisely a profile
likelihood ratio, and the likelihood engine was separately corrected for an
operator-precedence bug (see @sec-methods and the audit appendix). Window
sensitivity is reported transparently.

**Results.** A breakpoint near 2010 is confirmed for the UK and all constituent
nations except Northern Ireland. Depending on where the observation window ends,
the UK point slowdown is about `r hl_f`–`r repro_f`% (females) and
`r hl_m`–`r repro_m`% (males) of the earlier improvement rate; the 2011–2018
window reproduces the original paper's ~61%/61% exactly, and the strong 2019
recovery year lowers it. The point slowdown is real and sizeable, but formal
significance is reached for only `r n_sig` of 10 population–sex cells — UK and
England **males** (LR $p$ = `r f3(lr_get("United Kingdom","male", p_value))` and
`r f3(lr_get("England","male", p_value))`); every female cell and Northern
Ireland are consistent with a slowdown but not individually significant given
their noise. Because England is a large deterministic component of the UK, those
two significant cells are effectively **one** independent signal (annual-change
correlation ≈ `r f3(cor_uk_eng_m)`), not a cross-population pattern.
Descriptively, the 2020 pandemic shock lies far outside the model, and 2022–2024
improvement overshot the pre-2020 implied rate by about
`r f2(oos_overshoot("male"))`× before the shock and rebound partly cancel over
2020–2024. The newest ONS rounds (2020-, 2022-, 2024-based) sit close to the
pre-pandemic benchmark rather than far below it.

**Conclusion.** The stalling in UK $e_0$ improvement after 2010 was real and
roughly halved the earlier rate, but the evidence for it as a distinct
statistical signal rests on essentially one male series, and the partial
post-2020 recovery weakens any "stalling has only worsened" narrative. The value
of the index is transparency and timeliness between biennial ONS releases, not a
novel inferential apparatus.

# Introduction

Every couple of years the UK's ONS produces new national population projections,
including new assumptions about mortality and longevity. Such projections,
whether carried out by national statistical bodies or by private insurers, are
vital inputs to a wide range of decisions for the effective provision of state
services and assets, including schools, and social and healthcare needs at UK,
national and local levels.

Up until 2010, ONS forecasts of life-expectancy gains consistently
underestimated rates of improvement, and the assumptions were successively
uprated and made more optimistic in successive revisions [@ons_npp_accuracy].
Since 2010, however, the life-expectancy improvement assumptions made by the ONS
initially proved too optimistic, and were then successively made more pessimistic
for several revisions in a row; as we show below, the most recent rounds have
largely stabilised rather than continuing downward.

In parallel with the ONS' attempts to project life-expectancy trends, academic
demographers and commercial actuaries have also made predictions. A number of
approaches have been tried. The most technically sophisticated forecast the
individual components of life expectancy — mortality rates at individual ages —
and derive life expectancies from estimated life tables [@lee1992modeling], make
use of Bayesian methods for smoothing observations from neighbouring years and
age groups, and/or incorporate cohort effects allowing faster or slower gains in
some cohorts than others. An important UK example was the identification of a
so-called "Golden Cohort", persons born roughly between 1925 and 1945, whose
rates of mortality improvement appeared systematically higher than for earlier
or later cohorts, and which constituted a substantial source of "longevity risk"
for both private and state pensions.

Perhaps surprisingly, more complex approaches to demographic forecasting have
not been found to reliably outperform simpler approaches, and a very simple
approach to forecasting life expectancy, which does not involve forecasting
mortality at individual ages, has also been found to be effective
[@white2002longevity]. This approach simply assumes that life-expectancy
improvements will tend to continue linearly on average over the long term. This
assumption seems to hold more for the average of many similar populations, or
for the best-performing of a collection of high-income nations
[@oeppen2002broken], than for any single population [@lee2019mortality], but has
the dual advantages of simplicity and of allowing uncertainty intervals to be
generated from the observed variation in annual changes using well-established
time-series methods. This linear-trend view of life expectancy is the conceptual
starting point of the present paper.

Since around 2014, worsening trends in life-expectancy improvement have been an
increasing area of focus and concern in the UK among public-health researchers
and academics. Much of the surrounding commentary has focused on the role of
UK-government austerity policies and corresponding changes in the funding and
provision of out-of-work benefits and social and healthcare services; analyses
by others have instead emphasised the multifactorial nature of the slowdown and
the roles of influenza and slowing cardiovascular-disease improvement in
particular [@murphy2019stalling].

This paper focuses on how ONS mortality projections have changed over this period
of stalling UK life expectancy, and on how new annual data can be better used to
inform assumptions about future trajectories. We set out a simple, transparent
**monitoring index** for how substantial the post-2010 stalling has been: a
two-sample comparison of the mean annual $e_0$ change since 2010 against the
1991–2010 mean, accompanied by a likelihood-ratio test of whether the slowdown is
distinguishable from noise. The index can be recomputed within minutes of each
annual ONS release, so that a transparent interim summary of the underlying
improvement rate can be produced in the years between the biennial ONS releases.
Its contribution is timeliness and audit-grade reproducibility, not a novel
estimator: as we show in @sec-methods, the index reduces to a rescaled mean
comparison.

This is a **substantially revised analysis**. Relative to the original
2019-vintage draft it (i) extends the observed $e_0$ series from 2018 to 2024;
(ii) corrects an operator-precedence error in the likelihood engine (see
@sec-methods and the audit appendix); and (iii) recasts the estimator honestly as
a monitoring index — a profile likelihood ratio and its associated LR test —
rather than the "Bayes factor" of earlier drafts, and reports what formal
significance the data actually support. Two findings the extended data force upon
us shape the presentation: the point slowdown is sensitive to whether the
observation window ends in 2018 or 2019, and the 2020 pandemic year is not an
ordinary draw from the pre-pandemic process, so we compare (not validate) the
pre-pandemic estimate against 2020–2024 descriptively.

The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. We first place the UK slowdown in
international context (@sec-intl). We then examine UK-nation $e_0$ trends and
locate the breakpoint (@sec-uk). We present five decades of ONS projections
against observed $e_0$ (@sec-projns). We then give the monitoring-index estimate
of the slowdown with its significance test and transparent window sensitivity
(@sec-bf), compare the pre-pandemic estimate against 2020–2024 as a persistence
check (@sec-oos), and set the estimate against every ONS round from 2012 to 2024
(@sec-bfons). A discussion (@sec-discussion) synthesises and sets out
limitations.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

The Human Mortality Database (HMD) is a joint initiative of the Max Planck
Institute for Demographic Research, the University of California, Berkeley, and
INED (Paris), providing detailed mortality and population data produced under a
standard methodology for many populations [@hmd]. Period life expectancy at
birth ($e_0$) was extracted from the HMD to allow comparison between the UK and
other high-income nations, and from the ONS to allow comparison within UK
nations and groups.

Annual change in $e_0$ was computed across European and Anglophone nations to
assess the extent to which a slowdown in improvement is seen internationally, and
within UK nations to assess how similar the trends are within the UK. For UK
nations, changepoint analysis was performed using the `segmented`
[@muggeo2008segmented] and `changepoint` [@killick2014changepoint] R packages to
assess whether the slowdown is contemporaneous, which would suggest common
exposure. ONS projections from 2012 onwards are shown to demonstrate the extent
of the slowdown assumed by each biennial round.

**Actual $e_0$ series.** Values to 2018 are the ONS single-year life tables, as
used in the original paper [@ons_single_year_lifetables]. Because the ONS no
longer publishes single-year life tables beyond 2020, values for 2019–2024 are
taken from the historic estimates embedded in the 2024-based National Population
Projections (NPP) expectation-of-life files [@ons_expectation_of_life]. Over the
37 overlapping years (1982–2018) the two sources agree to within about 0.01
years on average, with the notable exception of Wales, which disagrees by up to
0.17 years (see @sec-discussion). The final actual point (2024) is the NPP
projection base year (mid-2024) and is therefore part-estimated.

**Monitoring-index definition.** For each population and sex we model annual
$e_0$ change as independent Normal draws. Calibrating on the annual changes for
1991–2010 (i.e. $e_0$ *levels* 1990–2010) gives a mean $\hat\mu_0$ and variance
$\hat\sigma^2$. For an observation window of post-2010 annual changes $x$ with
mean $\bar x$, the index summarises the slowdown by the ratio of the two means,

$$
\text{rate ratio} \;=\; \frac{\bar x}{\hat\mu_0},
\qquad
\text{slowdown \%} \;=\; 100\left(1 - \frac{\bar x}{\hat\mu_0}\right),
$$

so the estimator is simply a **two-sample comparison of the mean annual $e_0$
change** in the observation window against the calibration window. This is not
incidental: if one profiles a family of proportional-slowdown scenarios with
means $p\,\hat\mu_0$ ($0 \le p \le 1$) against the no-slowdown null $p=1$, the
maximising proportion is exactly $p^\star = \bar x / \hat\mu_0$ (clipped to
$[0,1]$), so the whole apparatus reduces to the mean ratio above. We treat this
transparency as the feature it is, rather than dressing it up as a bespoke
estimator.

**A note on the earlier framing.** Earlier drafts of this work described the
maximised likelihood ratio $\max_p \prod_i \phi(x_i; p\hat\mu_0,\hat\sigma^2) /
\prod_i \phi(x_i; \hat\mu_0,\hat\sigma^2)$ (with $\phi$ the Normal density) as a
"Bayes factor" and read its magnitude on the @kass1995bayes scale. With no prior
and no integration this quantity is a **profile likelihood ratio**, not a Bayes
factor, and the Kass–Raftery "positive/strong evidence" labels do not apply; we
therefore drop them. We retain the profile likelihood ratio (denoted PLR) only as
a continuity summary alongside the primary inferential quantity below. (This is a
separate matter from the likelihood-code bug documented next; see the audit
appendix for that history.)

**Significance test.** As the primary inferential summary we report a
likelihood-ratio test of $H_0\!:$ the observation-window mean equals the
calibration mean (no slowdown) against $H_1\!:$ the observation-window mean is
free, with the calibration variance treated as known. The statistic
$2\big(\ell(\bar x) - \ell(\hat\mu_0)\big)$ is referred to a $\chi^2_1$
distribution to give a $p$-value. This makes explicit what the profile likelihood
ratio only implies: whether the observed shortfall is distinguishable from the
noise in annual $e_0$ changes.

**Corrected likelihood.** The likelihood function in the original drafts
contained an operator-precedence error: the term intended as `1 / (2 * sig_sq)`
was written `(1 / 2 * sig_sq)`, which R evaluates as `0.5 * sig_sq`. Because the
first two terms of the Normal log-likelihood cancel in any likelihood ratio, the
ratio is affected only through the quadratic term, giving
$\log\mathrm{LR}_{\text{legacy}} = \sigma^4 \log\mathrm{LR}_{\text{correct}}$.
As $\sigma$ for annual $e_0$ change is roughly 0.1–0.25 years, this attenuated
every reported likelihood ratio toward 1 by three to four orders of magnitude,
which is why the original manuscript reported values indistinguishable from 1.
The *maximising* slowdown percentage is a monotone transform of the sum of
squares and is therefore **unaffected** by the fix; only the magnitudes change.
The corrected engine (`R/bayes_factors.R`) uses `dnorm`, and the monitoring index
(`R/monitoring_index.R`) is built on it; the fix and its impact on the original
2011–2018 findings are quantified in the audit appendix
(`audit/get_ll_fix_impact.qmd`).

**Pre-2020 headline and the 2020–2024 comparison.** The 2020–2021 pandemic years
are plainly not ordinary draws from the pre-pandemic process, and even 2019
already showed a recovery in improvement. We therefore treat a pre-pandemic
observation window (2011–2019) as the headline, alongside the 2011–2018 window
that reproduces the original analysis. We then compare — descriptively, not as a
forecast validation — the improvement rate the pre-pandemic data imply against
what 2020–2024 actually delivered. As shown in @sec-oos, the monitoring-index
identity means the "pre-2020 implied gain" *is* the 2011–2019 sample mean, so this
is a persistence check, not a test of forecast skill. For transparency we also
report a full series (2011–2024) and a COVID-excluded series (2011–2024 dropping
2020–2021), and do not privilege any single number without stating the others.

# Results 1: International context {#sec-intl}

Slowdowns in $e_0$ gain have been observed in a number of high-income nations in
recent years. On the (stale, ragged) HMD vintage used here the UK sits among the
slowest-improving high-income nations, alongside the USA, Iceland, the
Netherlands and Germany, but this comparison should be read with caution: the HMD
extract underlying @fig-intl ends around 2016 for most named comparators (and
2013–14 for some), whereas the UK series elsewhere in this paper runs to 2024, so
the "2010s" ordering is a truncated, country-specific window. We therefore do not
make a firm claim about the UK's *relative* severity here; refreshing the
comparison to a current common HMD vintage is flagged below and is being
undertaken separately. @fig-intl arranges HMD nations by their average annual
improvement in the 2010s. The nations with the fastest recent improvement are
Russia and Eastern European countries (e.g. Belarus, Ukraine, Russia, Lithuania,
Poland), while the slowest gains are seen in the USA, Iceland, the UK, the
Netherlands and Germany. In general, nations with the worst changes in the 1980s
and 1990s have tended to see the fastest improvement in the 2010s, and vice
versa. Notably, average improvement rates in Germany and the UK in the 2010s are
within about 0.01 years/year of one another.

```{r}
#| label: fig-intl
#| fig-cap: "Average annual change in period life expectancy at birth by decade across HMD high-income nations, arranged by average gain in the 2010s. Source: Human Mortality Database. (Figure regenerated in the 2026 refactor; see analysis/01_international_trends.qmd.)"
knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "A01_intl_mean_ch_e0_by_decade.png"))
```

A closer comparison of the slowest-improving high-income nations (the USA, the
UK, the Netherlands and Germany) is shown in @fig-intl-selected.

```{r}

knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "A02_selected_high_income.png"))
```

copying the original draft's truncated values.]

# Results 2: UK trends and the breakpoint {#sec-uk}

For the UK as a whole and all constituent nations except Northern Ireland, the
2000s saw faster improvement than the 1980s and 1990s, followed by a marked
slowdown in the 2010s. In the UK, improvement has been higher each decade for
males than for females. @tbl-uk-decades gives the UK decade means computed from
the extended ONS series.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-uk-decades
#| tbl-cap: "Mean annual change in UK period life expectancy at birth (years/year) by sex and period, from the extended ONS series. The 2020-24 mean is dominated by the single large 2020 fall (see text)."
uk_decades %>%
  mutate(m = round(m, 3)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = dec, values_from = m) %>%
  rename(Sex = sex) %>%
  select(Sex, `1980s`, `1990s`, `2000s`, `2011-19`, `2020-24`) %>%
  kbl() %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

The UK 2010s improvement (`r f3(uk_dec("female","2011-19"))` years/year for
females, `r f3(uk_dec("male","2011-19"))` for males) is roughly half the
1991–2010 calibration mean (`r f3(uk_calib_f)` female, `r f3(uk_calib_m)` male).
As shown in the annual series (@fig-uk-annual), the low 2010s average is not
driven by any single "bad year" but is part of a continuing trend; single years
in which $e_0$ fell are not in themselves exceptional, but a combination of
faster falls in bad years and lower gains in good years drives the slowdown.
Male and female trends within a nation tend to be more strongly correlated with
the same sex in other nations than with the opposite sex in the same nation, the
coupling being strongest in England and Wales and weakest in Northern Ireland.

```{r}
#| label: fig-uk-bar
#| fig-cap: "Average annual change in period life expectancy at birth in the UK and constituent nations, by sex and decade. Source: ONS."
knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "M01_ch_e0_uk_nations_barchart.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-uk-annual
#| fig-cap: "Annual change in period life expectancy at birth, UK and constituent nations, by sex. Source: ONS."
knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "A03_Annual_ch_uk_nations.png"))
```

To confirm that the 2010s represent a distinct break from previous trends,
breakpoint analysis was performed using segmented regression
[@muggeo2008segmented; @killick2014changepoint]. For the UK as a whole and all
constituent nations except Northern Ireland, a breakpoint in the series was
identified within one year of 2010 (@fig-breakpoint); for Northern Ireland a
breakpoint was instead identified in the mid-1980s. The contemporaneity of the
break across UK nations is consistent with a common exposure around 2010, broadly
consistent with previously published research on the UK stalling
[@murphy2019stalling].

```{r}
#| label: fig-breakpoint
#| fig-cap: "Segmented-regression breakpoints in annual life-expectancy change, UK and constituent nations. A break within one year of 2010 is found for all populations except Northern Ireland. Source: ONS."
knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "A10_brk_uk_nations.png"))
```

# Results 3: ONS projections against observed $e_0$ {#sec-projns}

@fig-fan shows ONS $e_0$ projection rounds from 1971 to 2024 against observed
$e_0$ (black). The picture is a three-act story of forecast error: successive
rounds *under*-predicted the $e_0$ actually achieved up until around 2010; from
2012 onwards the projections began instead to *over*-predict, with the 2008–2016
rounds now sitting well above observation; and the 2020-, 2022- and 2024-based
rounds start from the post-COVID level and are far more pessimistic in level than
anything before them, even as 2022–2024 show a partial recovery. This
self-contained figure is developed further as a standalone note
(`spinoff/forecasting_note.qmd`, "Fifty years of forecasting UK life
expectancy").

```{r}
#| label: fig-fan
#| fig-cap: "ONS UK life-expectancy projection rounds, 1971–2024 (coloured; darker = older rounds), against observed period life expectancy at birth (black). Each coloured line is one projection vintage extrapolating forward from its base year. The final actual point (2024) is the 2024-based NPP base year and is part-estimated. Source: ONS NPP accuracy report (1971–2012 rounds) and expectation-of-life datasets (2014–2024 rounds)."
knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "M02_ons_lt_projns_updated.png"))
```

The differences in projection *shape* reflect a range of methods: some early
projections are straight lines (consistent with simple linear $e_0$
extrapolation), whereas later projections are curved, reflecting assumptions
about age-specific mortality risks. Historically, projections built up from
age-specific rates have tended to underestimate achieved gains in high-income
countries. @tbl-ons-assumed reports the mean long-term annual $e_0$ improvement
assumed by each round from 2012 onwards. Even the 2012 round assumed rates below
the observed 1980s–2000s rates, so may have been considered conservative at the
time; each successive biennial round to 2018 assumed slower improvement than the
last. The extension of the table to the 2020-, 2022- and 2024-based rounds is
discussed in @sec-bfons, where it is set against the monitoring-index benchmark.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ons-assumed
#| tbl-cap: "Mean implied long-term annual e0 gain (years/year) by ONS projection round, UK. Computed from the projection period-e0 series in each round. Source: ONS expectation-of-life datasets 2012-2024 rounds."
uk_cmp %>%
  transmute(Round = round, Sex = sex, `Implied gain` = round(ons_mu, 3)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Sex, values_from = `Implied gain`) %>%
  arrange(Round) %>%
  kbl() %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

# Results 4: Monitoring-index estimate of the slowdown {#sec-bf}

This section quantifies how far post-2010 UK improvement has fallen short of the
1991–2010 trend, using the monitoring index of @sec-methods: the ratio of the
observation-window mean annual $e_0$ change to the calibration mean, with a
likelihood-ratio test of whether that shortfall is distinguishable from noise.
@fig-bf-schedules shows the profile-likelihood-ratio schedules for the
pre-pandemic window; the point slowdown is where each curve peaks.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bf-schedules
#| fig-cap: "Profile-likelihood-ratio schedules (log10 PLR against proposed percentage slowdown) for the pre-pandemic 2011-2019 window, by population and sex. Each curve peaks at the maximising slowdown; the height of the peak is the profile likelihood ratio, not a Bayes factor. (Figure generated by the earlier engine and labelled 'Bayes Factor'; the plotted quantity is the profile likelihood ratio.)"
knitr::include_graphics(rp("figures", "A12_Bayes_Factor_Schedules_2024.png"))
```

**Primary inferential summary.** @tbl-lr reports, for the 2011–2018 window that
reproduces the original analysis, the point slowdown, the rate ratio, the LR
statistic and its $p$-value, and the profile likelihood ratio, for every
population and sex.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lr
#| tbl-cap: "Monitoring index, 2011-2018 window (reproducing the original analysis), calibration 1991-2010. Slowdown % = 100(1 - rate ratio); rate ratio = observation-window mean / calibration mean annual e0 change. LR stat and p-value test 'some slowdown' vs 'no slowdown' (chi-square, 1 df). PLR is the profile likelihood ratio (the quantity earlier mislabelled a Bayes factor). Only UK and England males reach p<0.05."
lr_1118 %>%
  transmute(Population = population, Sex = sex,
            `Slowdown %` = round(slowdown_pct),
            `Rate ratio` = round(rate_ratio, 2),
            `LR stat` = round(lr_stat, 2),
            `p-value` = f3(p_value),
            PLR = round(plr, 1)) %>%
  kbl() %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

The point slowdown is real and sizeable everywhere except Northern Ireland — a
40–60% reduction on the earlier improvement rate across most cells — **but formal
significance is another matter**. Only `r n_sig` of the 10 population–sex cells
reach $p<0.05$: UK males ($p$ = `r f3(lr_get("United Kingdom","male", p_value))`)
and England males ($p$ = `r f3(lr_get("England","male", p_value))`). Every female
cell is consistent with a slowdown but not individually significant given its
noise — UK females $p$ = `r f3(lr_get("United Kingdom","female", p_value))`,
England females `r f3(lr_get("England","female", p_value))`, Scotland females
`r f3(lr_get("Scotland","female", p_value))`, Wales females
`r f3(lr_get("Wales","female", p_value))`, Northern Ireland females
`r f3(lr_get("Northern Ireland","female", p_value))` — and the remaining male
cells (Scotland `r f3(lr_get("Scotland","male", p_value))`, Wales
`r f3(lr_get("Wales","male", p_value))`, Northern Ireland
`r f3(lr_get("Northern Ireland","male", p_value))`) are likewise
non-significant. The proper reading is therefore: the *point* slowdown is large,
but the data support it as a distinct statistical signal only for males, and only
in the two most data-rich cells. Extending the window by one year to 2011–2019
leaves this pattern unchanged (UK males $p$ =
`r f3(lr_get("United Kingdom","male", p_value, lr_pre2020))`, England males $p$ =
`r f3(lr_get("England","male", p_value, lr_pre2020))`, all others
non-significant); the point slowdown falls (see window sensitivity below) but the
inference does not move.

**The two significant cells are one signal, not a pattern.** The apparent
"stronger evidence for males" must not be read as replication across populations.
The five populations are really about four nations — the UK is a deterministic
aggregate of its constituent nations, not an independent fifth series — and
**England dominates the UK**, accounting for roughly 84% of its population. The
UK-male and England-male annual-change series are almost perfectly correlated
(cor ≈ `r f3(cor_uk_eng_m)`), so the two significant cells are essentially **one**
independent observation, replicated by construction rather than by evidence. In
other words, the whole formal-significance case rests on a single male signal;
there is no cross-population corroboration, and no adjustment for having examined
several populations, both sexes and multiple windows would leave it looking
stronger.

**Window sensitivity.** @tbl-bf-maximise gives, for every population and sex, the
point slowdown percentage (and the $\log_{10}$ profile likelihood ratio at that
maximum) under the three observation-window variants. The point slowdown is
visibly window-sensitive; the significance pattern above is not.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bf-maximise
#| tbl-cap: "Point slowdown (% below the 1991-2010 mean improvement) and log10 profile likelihood ratio at the maximum, by observation-window variant. Pre-2020 is the headline; Full series and COVID-excluded are shown for transparency. These are point estimates, not evidence labels."
bf_argmax %>%
  mutate(cell = paste0(round(slowdown_pct), "% (", f2(log10_bf), ")")) %>%
  select(Population = population, Sex = sex, variant, cell) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = variant, values_from = cell) %>%
  arrange(Population, Sex) %>%
  kbl() %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Slowdown % (log10 PLR)" = 3))
```

Restricting the observation window to the pre-pandemic **2011–2018** span exactly
reproduces the original paper's headline — a `r repro_f`% slowdown for UK females
and `r repro_m`% for UK males, matching the original Table 4 — confirming that
the corrected engine and 2024-extended data recover the published result.
Extending the pre-pandemic window by the single further year **2019** — a strong
recovery year (UK $e_0$ rose 0.29 years for females and 0.24 for males, both
above the 1991–2010 mean) — already pulls the estimate down to **`r hl_f`%
(females) and `r hl_m`% (males)**. The original paper's headline was therefore,
unknowingly, sensitive to ending in 2018; 2019 already hinted at recovery before
COVID.

Reading across the variants for the UK reveals a genuine three-way tension. The
pre-pandemic headline points to roughly `r hl_f`%/`r hl_m`% (female/male). The
**full series to 2024 inflates this to `r full_f`%/`r full_m`%**, but that
inflation is driven almost entirely by the 2020 shock (UK $e_0$ fell 0.88 years
for females and 1.20 for males in 2020), which a Normal-iid likelihood wrongly
treats as an ordinary draw. Conversely, **excluding 2020–2021 pulls the estimate
down to `r cov_f`%/`r cov_m`%** — but this is not a clean "no slowdown" reading
either: it is pulled *up* by the genuine 2022–2024 recovery, which the original
2019-vintage analysis could not see. No single number is unambiguous; reporting
the full set of windows, together with the descriptive 2020–2024 comparison
(@sec-oos), is the most honest framing.

# Results 5: Persistence comparison against 2020–2024 {#sec-oos}

It is tempting to treat the pre-pandemic (2011–2019) window as a forecast and the
2020–2024 outturn as an out-of-sample validation of it. We resist that framing,
for two reasons. First, by the monitoring-index identity (@sec-methods) the
"pre-2020 implied gain" *is simply the 2011–2019 sample mean* — there is no
predictive distribution, no interval and no scoring rule, so comparing it to a
later mean is a **persistence check**, not a test of forecast skill. Second, the
pre-2020 window was itself chosen *after* seeing that 2019 recovered and 2020
crashed, so it is not a prospective forecast. @tbl-oos therefore sets the
pre-2020-implied gain against the 2020–2024 outturn descriptively, and @fig-oos
plots the same comparison.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-oos
#| tbl-cap: "Persistence comparison (not a validation): pre-pandemic (2011-2019) implied annual e0 gain -- which by the monitoring-index identity is the 2011-2019 mean -- against observed 2020-2024 changes (years/year). The 2024 actual is part-estimated (2024-based NPP base year)."
validation_table %>%
  transmute(Population = population, Sex = sex,
            `Pre-2020 implied` = round(implied_annual, 3),
            `Observed 2020` = round(obs_2020, 3),
            `Observed mean 2022-24` = round(obs_mean_2022_24, 3),
            `Observed mean 2020-24` = round(obs_mean_2020_24, 3)) %>%
  kbl() %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-oos
#| fig-cap: "Observed 2020-2024 annual e0 change (bars) against the pre-pandemic 2011-2019 mean annual gain (dashed line), by population and sex. This is a persistence comparison, not a forecast validation. The 2024 actual is part-estimated."
knitr::include_graphics(rp("figures", "A14_out_of_sample_validation_2024.png"))
```

Read honestly, the comparison neither confirms nor refutes a forecast — because
there was no probabilistic forecast to confirm. What it does show is two large
offsetting features. The **2020 shock** is far outside anything the pre-pandemic
mean contemplated (UK: `r f3(oos_g("female","obs_2020"))` years for females,
`r f3(oos_g("male","obs_2020"))` for males). The **2022–2024 recovery** then
*overshoots* the pre-2020 implied rate substantially: over 2022–2024 the UK
averaged `r f3(oos_g("female","obs_mean_2022_24"))` years/year for females and
`r f3(oos_g("male","obs_mean_2022_24"))` for males, about
`r f2(oos_overshoot("female"))`× and `r f2(oos_overshoot("male"))`× the pre-2020
implied gains of `r f3(oos_g("female","implied_annual"))` (female) and
`r f3(oos_g("male","implied_annual"))` (male). Averaged across the whole
2020–2024 window the shock and rebound roughly cancel (UK mean
`r f3(oos_g("female","obs_mean_2020_24"))` female,
`r f3(oos_g("male","obs_mean_2020_24"))` male), which is *why* the 5-year mean
happens to land near the pre-2020 rate — a coincidence of cancellation, not a
vindicated point forecast. The substantive message survives regardless of
framing: post-2020 improvement did not collapse further but rebounded, which
weakens any naive "the stalling has only worsened" narrative. A genuinely
prospective test would require pre-registering the implied rate and a scoring
rule *before* the data arrive; we flag this as the natural next step rather than
claiming it here. The 2022–2024 rebound should also be read with the
period-vs-cohort caveat of @sec-discussion in mind.

# Results 6: Comparison with ONS assumptions {#sec-bfons}

Finally we set the pre-pandemic monitoring-index benchmark — the pre-2020 implied
mean annual gain per population and sex — against the mean annual $e_0$
improvement implied by each ONS projection round from 2012 to 2024
[@ons_expectation_of_life]. Anchoring the comparison on the pre-pandemic window
(rather than a series including the COVID shock) keeps it clean: the ONS rounds
are themselves projections of a smoothly improving process. @tbl-bfons and
@fig-bfons give the comparison for the UK.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bfons
#| tbl-cap: "Mean implied annual e0 gain (years/year) by ONS round versus the fixed pre-pandemic monitoring-index benchmark, UK. A round below the benchmark projected slower improvement than the pre-2020 data implied (relatively pessimistic); above it, relatively optimistic. See text for the horizon-mismatch caveat."
uk_cmp %>%
  transmute(Round = round, Sex = sex,
            ONS = round(ons_mu, 3), `Index (pre-2020)` = round(bf_mu, 3)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Sex, values_from = c(ONS, `Index (pre-2020)`)) %>%
  select(Round, ONS_female, `Index (pre-2020)_female`, ONS_male, `Index (pre-2020)_male`) %>%
  arrange(Round) %>%
  kbl(col.names = c("Round", "ONS", "Index (pre-2020)", "ONS", "Index (pre-2020)")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Female" = 2, "Male" = 2))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bfons
#| fig-cap: "ONS-implied annual e0 gain by projection round (2012-2024) against the fixed pre-pandemic monitoring-index benchmark, UK. The benchmark is constant because it is the single pre-pandemic estimate."
knitr::include_graphics(rp("bayes_paper", "figures", "M03_ons_cf_bayes_2024.png"))
```

Reading down the UK block, the ONS rounds tracked steadily downwards from 2012,
reflecting the accumulating evidence of stalling: for UK females the implied gain
fell from `r f3(uk_get("female", 2012))` years/year (2012 round) toward the
pre-pandemic benchmark of `r f3(bf_f)`, and for males from
`r f3(uk_get("male", 2012))` toward `r f3(bf_m)`.

On its face the newest rounds appear to have **stabilised close to the pre-2020
benchmark rather than continuing far below it**. For UK females the 2020-, 2022-
and 2024-based rounds imply `r f3(uk_get("female", 2020))`,
`r f3(uk_get("female", 2022))` and `r f3(uk_get("female", 2024))` years/year
respectively — all at or slightly *above* the benchmark of `r f3(bf_f)`. For UK
males the same rounds imply `r f3(uk_get("male", 2020))`,
`r f3(uk_get("male", 2022))` and `r f3(uk_get("male", 2024))`, straddling the
benchmark of `r f3(bf_m)`. The sharp downward revision therefore happened over
the 2012–2018 rounds and appears to have since levelled off; the fan figure's
apparent "sharp pessimism" of the newest rounds (@fig-fan) is about the post-COVID
starting *level*, not the assumed *rate* of future gain.

This "stabilised near the benchmark" reading, however, needs an important caveat.
The ONS-implied gain here is the mean annual $e_0$ change over each round's
*entire ~50-year projection horizon*, whereas the benchmark is a *near-term*
(pre-2020) rate. Because annual $e_0$ gains decline over a projection horizon
(rectangularisation) even at constant assumed mortality-improvement rates, a
50-year average sits mechanically below the near-term rate — so part of the
apparent convergence could be an artefact of the summary statistic rather than a
genuine matching of assumptions. A cleaner comparison would recompute the
ONS-implied gain over a matched near-term horizon (the first ~8–10 projection
years), or compare age-specific assumed improvement rates directly. [TODO:
recompute @tbl-bfons and @fig-bfons on a matched near-term horizon before
leaning hard on the "stabilised near the benchmark" claim.] With that caveat, the
defensible statement is the weaker one: the original draft's characterisation
that the ONS "may still be underestimating the stalling, especially for females"
is not supported by the latest rounds, which are at least broadly consistent
with the pre-pandemic evidence rather than clearly more optimistic.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

This paper set out to quantify the post-2010 slowdown in UK life-expectancy
improvement using a transparent, rapidly-updatable monitoring index, and — in a
substantial revision of the original analysis — to compare a pre-pandemic
estimate descriptively against the 2020–2024 outturn.

The central findings are threefold. First, the stalling around 2010 was real: a
breakpoint within a year of 2010 is confirmed for the UK and all constituent
nations except Northern Ireland, and the pre-pandemic monitoring index puts the
UK point slowdown at roughly `r hl_f`% (females) to `r repro_m`% (males) of the
earlier improvement rate, reproducing the original ~61% exactly for the 2011–2018
sub-window. But the *point* estimate and its *statistical significance* are
different things: recast as likelihood-ratio tests, only `r n_sig` of 10
population–sex cells reach $p<0.05$ (UK and England males), all female cells and
Northern Ireland are non-significant, and — because England is ~84% of the UK and
the two significant series correlate ≈ `r f3(cor_uk_eng_m)` — those two cells are
effectively **one** independent signal, not a cross-population pattern. Second,
this point estimate is genuinely window-sensitive: the strong 2019 recovery year
lowers it by around ten points, the 2020 shock inflates the full-series estimate,
and excluding the pandemic years lowers it again — so no single number is clean,
and the honest presentation is the full set of windows plus the descriptive
2020–2024 comparison. Third, the 2022–2024 recovery, invisible to the original
2019-vintage analysis, has returned improvement to (and briefly above) the
reduced-but-positive rate the pre-2020 data implied, and the newest ONS rounds
sit close to that same benchmark (subject to the horizon caveat of @sec-bfons).
Together these weaken a naive "the stalling has only worsened" narrative and
soften the original policy implication.

The **correction of the likelihood bug** does not change any maximising slowdown
percentage — those are monotone in the sum of squares — but it restores
meaningful likelihood-ratio magnitudes and, in doing so, reverses the original
draft's sex emphasis. What signal there is is carried by males rather than
females (the female series being noisier relative to their smaller mean gain), so
the original draft's suggestion that the ONS remained too optimistic *mainly* for
females does not survive. This is a statement about which series carries the
signal, not an "evidence-strength" label: with no prior and no integration the
quantity is a profile likelihood ratio, so we do not read it on the
@kass1995bayes scale, and the formal case for a distinct slowdown signal rests on
the single male cell described above. Any previously circulated numbers quoting
"Bayes-factor" *magnitudes* or Kass–Raftery evidence labels should be treated as
superseded by the likelihood-ratio $p$-values reported here and by the audit
appendix.

**Value of the index.** The monitoring index can be recomputed within minutes of
each annual ONS release, providing a transparent interim estimate of the
underlying improvement rate in the years between the biennial NPP rounds. Its
contribution is timeliness and audit-grade reproducibility, not a novel
estimator — it is, transparently, a two-sample comparison of means. A commitment
to publish an updated index on each release — made *before* the data are seen —
would turn the descriptive comparison of @sec-oos into a genuinely prospective
test, and would give researchers and policymakers a shared "ground truth" around
which to reason even where they disagree about causes.

**Limitations.** Several caveats bound the conclusions. (i) The Normal-iid
likelihood treats every annual change as an exchangeable draw, which the 2020
pandemic year plainly is not; we address this pragmatically by holding the
pandemic years out of the headline and reporting window sensitivity, rather than
by modelling a level shift or outlier explicitly — a natural extension. (We note
in passing that annual $e_0$ changes are in fact negatively autocorrelated
(lag-1 ≈ −0.5), so the iid assumption is, if anything, *conservative* for the
headline significance and does not inflate it.) (ii) **Period vs cohort, and
harvesting.** The outcome is *period* life expectancy at birth, a synthetic
cross-sectional index, not the realised lifespan of any cohort. This matters
directly for the paper's headline update: a mortality shock like 2020 depletes
the frailest of the older population, so the following years' *period* rates
mechanically improve as the depleted-frail cohort produces fewer deaths — a
"harvesting" rebound. The 2022–2024 recovery that we present as weakening the
"stalling has only worsened" narrative is therefore at genuine risk of being, in
part, a harvesting artefact of a synthetic index rather than a return of
underlying mortality improvement; the two are not distinguishable from period
$e_0$ alone. All recovery claims here should be read as statements about *period
$e_0$ as a demographic index*; adjudicating harvesting versus genuine improvement
would require a cohort, decomposition or lifespan-variation lens that this
monitoring index does not provide. (iii) Multiple populations, both sexes and
several windows were examined; as set out in @sec-bf the two significant cells are
one signal by construction, so no individual cell should be read as independent
confirmatory evidence. (iv) The actual $e_0$ series splices two ONS sources;
these agree closely except for **Wales**, where the single-year life tables and
the NPP-embedded historic estimates disagree by up to ~0.17 years, likely because
of population-estimate revisions following the 2021 census — so the Welsh
estimates in particular should be treated with caution. (v) The final actual
point (2024) is the NPP projection base year and is part-estimated. (vi) The
calibration and comparison rest on a single pre-slowdown window (1991–2010); the
qualitative picture is robust, but the exact percentages depend on that choice.
(vii) The international comparison (@sec-intl) rests on a pre-2017 HMD vintage on
a ragged window and is not current; the relative-severity ordering should not be
quoted until it is refreshed.

**Policy reading.** The original work concluded that the most recent ONS forecast
still appeared too optimistic and underestimated the UK slowdown. The extended,
corrected analysis qualifies this. The point slowdown was real and roughly halved
the earlier improvement rate, but the formal evidence for it as a distinct
statistical signal rests on essentially one male series, and the post-pandemic
recovery together with the stabilisation of the newest ONS rounds mean that, for
the latest vintages, the ONS assumptions are broadly consistent with the
pre-pandemic evidence rather than clearly too optimistic. We make no firm claim
here about the UK's severity *relative* to other high-income nations, which the
repo's current (stale) international data cannot support. Whether the modest
2022–2024 recovery reflects genuine underlying improvement rather than a period
harvesting rebound — and whether the drivers of the post-2010 stall have been
addressed — remains open, and is exactly the kind of question the
rapidly-updatable index is well suited to track as each new year of data
arrives.

# References {.unnumbered}
